<<< fixed section: recovery scams >>>
== Watch out for recovery scams (DRAFT, not yet approved) ==
After a loss, people are often contacted by someone who says they can get the money back: a "recovery service", a "blockchain investigator", a lawyer, or someone claiming to be from a government agency. Many of these are a second scam aimed at the same victim.

  - No one can reverse a confirmed blockchain transaction. Funds come back only when an exchange or issuer freezes them and a court or law enforcement acts.
  - Law enforcement agencies do not charge fees to recover funds, and they do not ask for payment in crypto, gift cards or wire transfers.
  - Be wary of anyone who contacts you first, asks for an upfront fee, asks for your wallet's recovery phrase or private key, or asks you to install remote-access software.
  - TraceAWallet will never contact you to offer recovery, and never asks for payment.

If someone offers recovery, report the contact at ic3.gov as well.
<<< end of fixed section >>>

<<< fixed section: IC3 checklist >>>
== Filing with the FBI's IC3 (DRAFT, not yet approved) ==
The FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center takes reports at ic3.gov. Gather these before you start:

  [ ] Each payment you made: the date, the amount, the asset (for example USDT on Tron) and the transaction hash
  [ ] The address you sent from, and the address you sent to (this report's address: 0xc76afbf0f69ae9be5d855239c50673252cf3f26b on Ethereum)
  [ ] The exchange or wallet app you sent from, and your account details there
  [ ] The names, usernames, phone numbers, email addresses and websites the other party used
  [ ] Messages, screenshots and any documents they sent you
  [ ] The platform or app you were told to use, with its web address

After filing:
  [ ] Keep the complaint ID IC3 gives you
  [ ] Tell the exchange or wallet provider you sent from, and give them the IC3 complaint ID
  [ ] Consider a report to your local police as well
<<< end of fixed section >>>
